Pinned .NET docs only list the name ("- Liskov substitution principle") without a formulation; no official source in versions.yaml defines it, and the lesson adds no specific rule beyond the definition.

git show stage-1:.../Oop/ShippingFee.cs: abstract class ShippingFee { public abstract int ForOrder(int totalVnd); }; StandardShipping => totalVnd >= 2_000_000 ? 0 : 30_000; ExpressShipping => 60_000; PickUpInStore => 0. No throw anywhere, so every int input yields an int. override.md: "An `override` method must have the same signature as the overridden base method. `override` methods support covariant return types." tips-for-java-developers.md: "C# doesn't have the concept of *checked exceptions*. Any method might (in theory) throw any exception." Covariant returns do not affect this int-returning case.

git show stage-1:.../SamplesTests.cs lines 18-24: var kinds = new ShippingFee[] { new StandardShipping(), new ExpressShipping(), new PickUpInStore() }; Assert.Equal(new[] { 0, 60_000, 0 }, kinds.Select(kind => kind.ForOrder(2_000_000))). Block matches exactly.

Traced from ShippingFeeLspViolation.cs:14,22-23: StandardShippingOk(500_000): 500_000 >= 2_000_000 false -> 30_000; (6_000_000) -> 0. BulkOnlyShipping(6_000_000): >= 5_000_000 -> 45_000; (500_000) -> throw new InvalidOperationException("order too small for bulk shipping").
Line 23 uses `totalVnd >= 5_000_000 ? 45_000 : throw ...`; 5_000_000 satisfies >=, so a test asserting 45_000 at exactly 5,000,000 passes while every total below throws.
